Lectio · The First Project

# Let any person read a great work. *With genuine ease.*

Lectio is a reader for the great books. Each one gets a new edition in plain current English, faithful to the original, with the historical translations and the original language one tap away.

It is the first project of the San Diego Institute of Technology. 17 editions are in beta. The app is not out yet. This page says where everything stands.

## The greatest books ever written are almost entirely unread.

People are capable of reading them. What stops them is the way in.

The great works are free and in the public domain: *The Iliad*, *Meditations*, *The Divine Comedy*, the *Tao Te Ching*. Almost nobody reads them.

The free copy of each is a translation a century or more old. Its English puts even a native speaker at a distance, and its names and references assume a classical schooling few people have now. Most reading apps hand over the same 1909 file and leave you to it.

Lectio gives each book a clear modern edition and keeps the old ones beside it. It is the whole book, made for the reader it has now. Nothing is cut and nothing is summarized.

## The books that have a Lectio edition today.

Each cover opens a page on that edition: what the book is, why the edition was made, how it begins, the choices it makes, and the record of how it was drafted and checked.

- [ Meditations Marcus Aurelius ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/)
- [ The Iliad Homer ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/)
- [ The Odyssey Homer ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/odyssey/)
- [ The Republic Plato ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/)
- [ The Aeneid Virgil ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/)
- [ The Prince Niccolò Machiavelli ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/)
- [ The Analects Confucius ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/)
- [ The Tao Te Ching Laozi ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/tao-te-ching/)
- [ The Dhammapada Early Buddhist tradition ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/dhammapada/)
- [ The Bhagavad Gita ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/bhagavad-gita/)
- [ The Epic of Gilgamesh Sumer & Akkad ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/gilgamesh/)
- [ Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/nicomachean-ethics/)
- [ Confessions Saint Augustine ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/confessions/)
- [ The Divine Comedy Dante Alighieri ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/divine-comedy/)
- [ Hamlet William Shakespeare ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/hamlet/)
- [ The Gospel of Mark attributed to Mark ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mark/)
- [ Genesis Ancient Israel ](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/genesis/)

**Where these stand:** All 17 are beta. They were drafted by AI models. In November 2026 every section had a first review by machine readers, and the confirmed fixes were applied. An edition becomes a release through [the review of its readers](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#scholars) together with the editor's own full read. Neither has happened yet for any edition. [How an edition is made.](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mission/)

## What readable means.

The opening of *Meditations*, Book II. A Roman emperor is telling himself how to face the morning.

**George Long · 1862**

> Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.

**Lectio Edition · 2026**

> Begin each morning by telling yourself: today I will meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, envious, and unsociable. They are like this because they cannot tell good from evil.

The first is the edition most people meet. It is accurate, and it was written for readers who died a century ago. The second is the same two sentences as they stand in the Lectio Edition today. In the app, Long, Casaubon's English of 1634 and the Greek stay beside it.

## How an edition is made.

A Lectio edition is a new rendering of the whole work. It is drafted by an AI model and it says so.

The public-domain translations and, where we have it, the original are brought into one bundle. A model drafts the edition section by section. A second reader, also a model, then reads every section against those sources and reports what is wrong. A further pass tries to prove each finding false, and only the fixes that survive are applied. At that point the edition is a beta. It becomes a release when its readers have reviewed it and the editor has read the whole of it himself. Neither has happened yet for any book.

Each edition is stamped with the year it was drafted and the date it was last revised, and it carries its sources and the places where it departs from the older English.

[The translation mission, in full](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mission/)

## About twenty books at launch. Then one each Monday.

This is the plan. Dates can slip. The launch books go out as betas. A book that is not finished does not go out.

The launch shelf is 20 books: the 17 above and 3 more that are drafted and not yet in the library, *Apology, Crito & Phaedo* (Plato), *The Art of War* (Sun Tzu) and *The Golden Sayings* (Epictetus).

After launch, one new book appears each Monday from January 4, 2027, announced in [the Daily](https://sandiegotech.org/daily.html). The first 12 are dated. The register behind them holds 219 books in all.

## The app is built and not yet released.

Lectio is being prepared for the App Store. The Institute's Apple developer enrollment is in review, and nothing can be submitted until it clears. When the app is out it will be free.

It runs on iPhone and iPad. It opens to the books you have been reading. Every book lists its editions, and switching between them keeps your place. You can set a passage beside the same passage in another edition, and keep bookmarks, highlights, notes and saved words.

There is no link here because there is nothing to install yet. The Daily will say when there is.

## Printed editions are planned. One proof exists.

The printed book is set from the same bundle the app reads, so the page and the screen carry the same text.

The only printed artifact today is a proof of *Meditations*. Only a release is printed, and the editor reads the proof on paper before it is sold. The plan after that is one printed edition a month, shortest works first.

The text will be free to read, in the app and as a PDF. The bound book is what is sold, and what it earns goes to the Institute. One PDF exists today, of *Meditations*: [PDF, beta, revised November 2026](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/meditations-lectio-edition-2026-11.pdf).

Editions in other languages are planned, Spanish first. None exists yet beyond a trial setting of *Meditations*.

## Every edition is beta until its readers make it a release.

A Lectio edition is labeled beta from the day it is made. It earns its release stamp through the review of its readers, students and scholars alike, together with the editor's own full read.

This is review by care, not by credential. A scholar here is anyone who will read closely. You hold the Lectio edition against the older translations, or against the original if you have the language. You flag where a passage loses the sense or reads badly, and you say so plainly.

Every flagged passage anchors to an exact segment of the text. An accepted correction lands in the next revision with its reason recorded. A released edition names its reviewers in the colophon. Only releases go to print.

There is a precedent. The Oxford English Dictionary began with an appeal to the public, and volunteer readers spent decades mailing quotation slips to its editors. Lectio works the same way, with better instruments.

The machine review of November 2026 was a first pass. It does not replace this one. No edition has had its readers' review yet.

[Join the review](mailto:brandon@sandiegotech.org?subject=Lectio%20Scholars&body=I%27d%20like%20to%20join%20the%20review.%0A%0AA%20work%20I%27d%20want%20to%20read%20closely%3A%20)

**Open now:** The first open review is *Meditations*. The beta is on [its edition page](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/), and the whole text is here to read: [PDF, beta, revised November 2026](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/meditations-lectio-edition-2026-11.pdf).

## The method and the record are public.

Each edition's page carries its own record: the model that drafted it, its sources, what the review found and fixed, and what is still open.

If you read a passage and think it is wrong, write to [brandon@sandiegotech.org](mailto:brandon@sandiegotech.org?subject=Lectio) and say where.

Lectio · The Translation Mission

# A new edition of each great book, and an account of how it was made.

This page is the method, told once. It covers why Lectio makes new editions at all, what they are held to, the stages each goes through, what the first full review found, and what is still undone.

It describes things as they are on November 17, 2026.

## Why make a new edition at all.

Most of these books were never English. Every English reader has only ever met Homer, Plato or Laozi in translation, and a translation belongs to its time.

The translations that are free to print are old. Pope's Iliad is from 1715. Long's Marcus Aurelius is from 1862. They are good, and some are great. But their English has moved away from us. Old translations use old words, and they also use words we still use in senses we no longer mean. "Temperance" now suggests not drinking. "Piety" suggests church. "Idea" suggests a thought in someone's head.

The good modern translations are under copyright. They cannot be given away, and they cannot be set beside each other in one reader.

So the choice for a free reader was to hand people the 1909 file, or to make something new. Lectio makes a new edition and keeps the old ones next to it. The older translations and the original are not replaced. They are there to be read, and the new edition is how most people will get to them.

## What "modern" means here.

A Lectio edition must read for anyone from about fifteen to ninety.

That rule decides the vocabulary. The English is plain and current, and it is never fashionable. A word half the readers would have to look up is a failure, and so is a word that will sound dated in ten years. The editions draw on the durable middle of the language, the part three generations share.

It cuts both ways. The first review took out "girlfriend", "the haves" and "for free". It also took out "car" for chariot, "chine" and "yonder".

Modern does not mean casual, and it does not mean simplified. Aristotle's distinctions are all still there. Machiavelli is as cold as he was.

## Faithful to the original, and complete.

A Lectio edition is the whole work, in order, at its own length. It is a translation in the ordinary sense. The claim is that someone who has read the Lectio *Iliad* has read the *Iliad*.

Fidelity is checked clause by clause: anything added, dropped, softened, sharpened, or explained. An explanation written into the author's sentence counts as an error even when it is correct. What a reader needs to know goes in a note beside the text.

Names stay. Famous lines stay recognizable. Verse keeps its lines. Where an author repeats a phrase on purpose, the English repeats it.

Shakespeare is the exception that shows the rule. He wrote in English, so there the edition changes very little and his own text stays the default.

## What is reproduced, and what is only consulted.

Public-domain texts are reproduced in full. Copyrighted work is never reproduced.

- **Public-domain translations** are included whole in the app, with translator and year: Pope, Butler, Dryden, Jowett, Long, Legge, Longfellow, the King James translators and others.
- **Original-language texts** are included where we have brought them in. Today that is the Greek of *Meditations* and Shakespeare's own *Hamlet*. The rest are still to come.
- **Modern translations and scholarship under copyright** are named in an edition's provenance where they were consulted. Their text is not quoted or reproduced, in the app or on this site.
- **The Lectio edition** is the Institute's own text, released under CC BY-NC 4.0.

Copyright protects a translator's wording. It does not protect what a passage means. That is the line the editions keep to, and it is the same line any scholar keeps.

Every edition carries a provenance record: the model that drafted it, the date, the sources, and the method. An edition without one does not ship. A Lectio edition is never presented as a historical translation.

## The six stages an edition goes through.

The first four are done by machine and produce a beta. The fifth belongs to people and cannot be handed to a model.

1. **Ingest.** The public-domain translations and the original are brought into the bundle, each with its source and rights recorded.
2. **Draft.** An AI model writes the Lectio rendering, one section at a time.
3. **Review.** A second reader takes each section and reads it against every other edition of that section. It checks fidelity first, then register, voice, how the sentences read aloud, and form. It grades the section A, B or C and lists each fault with the source reading and a proposed fix.
4. **Fix.** A further pass takes each reported fault and tries to prove it wrong. Only what holds is kept. The fix is written to change as little of the sentence as it needs.
5. **Readers' review and the editor's read.** Readers hold the beta against the older translations or the original and flag what is wrong. The editor reads the whole edition and the list of fixes, and strikes what he does not want.
6. **Release.** The corrections are applied, the bundle is rebuilt, and the edition is stamped a release. Only a release is printed.

**Where the 17 editions are:** All 17 are beta. They have been through the first four stages. In this first run the editor chose to apply every confirmed fix before reading, so the corrected text is what the bundle now holds. The fifth stage has not been done for any of them: no readers' review has closed and the editor has not yet read any edition in full. 0 of 17 are releases.

## What the first full review found.

In November 2026 every drafted edition was read against its sources: 17 works, 442 sections, about a million words.

No section had to be redone. 212 sections were graded A, meaning no changes proposed. 230 were graded B, meaning small fixes. None was graded C. The readers found 51 errors of meaning, about 480 places where a reader would stumble, and roughly twice as many points of polish.

After each finding was re-checked, 2,208 fixes were applied: 113 high, 752 medium and 1,343 low. High means the meaning was wrong or missing. Medium means a reader would stumble. Low is polish. The count of high fixes is larger than the count of errors because one decision, such as a single English word for a key term, becomes many entries.

| Edition | Drafted by | Sections | A | B | High | Medium | Low |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Meditations](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 12 | 0 | 12 | 8 | 45 | 102 |
| [The Iliad](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 24 | 4 | 20 | 5 | 44 | 114 |
| [The Odyssey](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/odyssey/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 24 | 5 | 19 | 2 | 31 | 250 |
| [The Republic](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/#made) | Fable 5 | 10 | 1 | 9 | 28 | 75 | 76 |
| [The Aeneid](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 12 | 0 | 12 | 8 | 62 | 74 |
| [The Prince](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/#made) | Fable 5 | 26 | 20 | 6 | 0 | 15 | 28 |
| [The Analects](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/#made) | Fable 5 | 20 | 14 | 6 | 0 | 15 | 150 |
| [The Tao Te Ching](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/tao-te-ching/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 81 | 65 | 16 | 4 | 26 | 30 |
| [The Dhammapada](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/dhammapada/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 26 | 6 | 20 | 3 | 31 | 49 |
| [The Bhagavad Gita](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/bhagavad-gita/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 18 | 8 | 10 | 3 | 24 | 49 |
| [The Epic of Gilgamesh](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/gilgamesh/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 11 | 0 | 11 | 2 | 23 | 48 |
| [Nicomachean Ethics](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/nicomachean-ethics/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 10 | 0 | 10 | 38 | 112 | 56 |
| [Confessions](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/confessions/#made) | Fable 5 | 13 | 2 | 11 | 1 | 18 | 55 |
| [The Divine Comedy](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/divine-comedy/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 100 | 55 | 45 | 2 | 134 | 171 |
| [Hamlet](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/hamlet/#made) | Opus 4.8 | 5 | 0 | 5 | 9 | 67 | 71 |
| [The Gospel of Mark](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mark/#made) | Opus 5 | 16 | 3 | 13 | 0 | 27 | 8 |
| [Genesis](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/genesis/#made) | Opus 5 | 34 | 29 | 5 | 0 | 3 | 12 |
| Total |  | 442 | 212 | 230 | 113 | 752 | 1,343 |

The readers were AI models, up to twenty working at once. For most works the original language is not yet in the bundle, so the reader compared the draft with the public-domain translation and judged the original from its own knowledge of it. Each edition's page says which was the case. That is a real limit, and it is one reason the editor's read matters.

### The five causes

The same five causes account for most of what was found.

1. **The older translator's notes printed as the author.** Footnotes and bracketed glosses from the base translation had been carried into the text. In *Meditations*, a footnote of George Long's quoting Homer was printed as Marcus's own words. A translator's note sat inside the Muses' speech in the *Republic*.
2. **Drafted from the English, not the original.** Where the base translation was wrong or coy, so was the draft. Marcus's grandfather's mistress had become his father's.
3. **No style sheet.** Each section was drafted alone, so names and key terms changed from book to book. The *Ethics* had four English words for temperance. *The Prince* kept "virtù" in some chapters and translated it in others.
4. **Explanation written into the sentence.** A gloss after a name. A moral after an ending.
5. **Single words in the wrong register.** Too new on one side, too old on the other.

### What changed in the method

- A style sheet is written before the first section: names, the dozen key terms and the one English word for each, oaths, quotation and verse style, what stays in the original language. The rules the reviewers wrote for each work, which are on each edition's page, are the first of these.
- New editions are drafted from the original, with the public-domain translation as a check on meaning and not as the text to modernize. The original is to be bundled for every work so that review can check against it.
- The build gets a mechanical gate: no brackets or translator's notes in a Lectio segment, one quotation style per work.
- 9 segments that turned out to be an editor's note or an invented sentence are now marked so the app, print and audio skip them. Segment numbers are frozen, so they could not simply be deleted.
- Quoted verse inside prose is to keep its line breaks. The build does not do this yet.

## The readers' review.

Every edition is beta until its readers make it a release. The review is open to anyone who will read closely, students and scholars alike. It is review by care, not by credential.

A reviewer holds the Lectio edition against the older translations or the original, flags where a passage loses the sense or reads badly, and says so plainly. Each flag anchors to an exact segment. An accepted correction lands in the next revision with its reason recorded, and a released edition names its reviewers in the colophon.

The machine review described above came first and does not replace this. The first open review is *Meditations*.

[The Scholars, and how to join](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#scholars)

## Which models, and why.

Each edition names the model that drafted it. The first review also gave a way to compare them.

| Drafted by | Works | Serious and medium faults per 10,000 words | Errors of meaning per 100,000 words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Opus 4.8 (June 2026) | 11 | 6.3 | 6.8 |
| Fable 5 (July 2026) | 4 | 2.1 | 1.4 |

The works differ, so this is suggestive and not proof. But the stronger model made about a third as many faults and a fifth as many errors of meaning, and errors of meaning are the ones that matter. The table covers fifteen works. The other two, Genesis and Mark, were drafted by a different model (Claude Opus 5) under their own charter and are not in the comparison.

From this the plan follows. Draft with the best model available, because drafting is done once and read by everyone after. Do the first review with a model that reads closely and can run many sections at once. Do the fix pass on the best model, because it decides what prints.

The changes to the method matter more than any change of model.

## One edition, stamped, with revisions.

An edition carries a vintage, the year it was drafted, and a revision date. All 17 editions are vintage 2026, revised November 17, 2026, and beta.

Fixes from review are revisions. The vintage stays the same, the revision date changes, and each change is logged. An edition is revised in the open. It is not quietly regenerated.

A new vintage is a full redraft, and it is made only when it is measurably better. Three sections are redrafted as a trial and reviewed blind against the current text. The trial has to win on faults per ten thousand words and on the editor's own reading. Otherwise the current edition stands. The trial is run about once a year, when a new generation of models arrives. Some years nothing will change.

Old vintages are kept with their provenance, so a passage can still be cited from the edition it came from. The printed book carries its vintage and revision in the colophon.

## The review record, and where to read it.

For every work the review left a record: a report on each section, the list of fixes with the reason for each, the rules chosen for the work, the findings that were rejected and why, and what was left for the editor.

Each edition's page on this site gives the substance of it: the model and drafting date, the sources, what the edition was checked against, the grades, the fixes by severity, the rules, and a plain list of what is still open. Start from [the library](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#library).

The files themselves are in the Lectio repository under `review/`. If you find an error in an edition, write to [brandon@sandiegotech.org](mailto:brandon@sandiegotech.org?subject=Lectio) with the passage.

## Other languages.

Translation has always carried these books from one language and one century into the next. English is the first language Lectio works in. It is not meant to be the only one.

Spanish comes first. A translation starts only from an edition that is a release. It is made from the original, with the Lectio English as the guide to register. It needs its own reader at the read stage, a native speaker. It is a new edition of the same work under the same rules.

A Spanish *Meditations* has been set as a print trial and is not finished. There will be no second language until the first has a reader.

## What is not done yet.

An account of a method should say where it stops.

- The readers' review and the editor's read. No edition has had either in full, so all 17 are beta. Each edition's page lists what waits for the editor. *Meditations* is first.
- One house style across works. Each edition is now consistent within itself, but they differ from each other in quotation marks and dashes.
- The originals. Only two works have their original text in the bundle.
- The margin notes. Explanations that were taken out of the text have mostly not yet been written as notes.
- The launch shelf. 3 drafted books still have to be brought into the library and reviewed.
- The app's release, which waits on Apple.
- Print, beyond one proof. Other languages, beyond one trial.

[Back to the library](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#library)

Lectio Edition · 2026

# Meditations

Marcus Aurelius

- 170–180 CE
- Western tradition
- Philosophy
- Lectio Edition 2026

The private notebook of a Roman emperor. Marcus Aurelius wrote it in Greek, at night and on campaign, to remind himself how to live: with reason, with justice, and without fear of death. He did not mean anyone to read it.

## A man talking to himself should sound like one.

Most readers meet Marcus in George Long's translation of 1862. It is accurate and it is stiff. "Begin the morning by saying to thyself" is not how anyone speaks to himself, and the book is nothing but a man speaking to himself.

The older English also carries its own furniture. Long's brackets, footnotes and conjectures sit in and around the text, and a reader cannot always tell where Marcus stops and his translator begins.

The Lectio Edition gives the twelve books in plain current English, with nothing in the text that the Greek does not have. Long, Casaubon's English of 1634 and the Greek itself stay in the app beside it. The aim is that you read Marcus straight through, and go to the older versions when a line makes you curious.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · What I Learned, and From Whom**

> From my grandfather Verus, I learned to be good-natured and to keep my temper under control.

> From everything I heard and remembered about my father, I learned modesty and a strong, manly character.

> From my mother, I learned reverence and generosity; to hold back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking it; and to live simply, far from the habits of the rich.

> From my great-grandfather, I learned the value of not relying on public schools but having good teachers at home—and that this is something worth spending freely on.

> From my tutor, I learned not to back the Greens or the Blues at the races, or the small-shield or the big-shield fighters in the arena; to endure hard work, to want little, to do things with my own hands, to mind my own business, and to refuse to listen to gossip.

> From Diognetus, I learned not to waste myself on trivial things; not to believe the claims of magicians and quacks about spells and exorcisms; and not to keep quails for fighting, or get excited about such things. He taught me to put up with plain speaking and to take philosophy seriously; he led me to hear the philosophers Bacchius, Tandasis, and Marcianus, to write dialogues as a boy, and to choose the simple camp-bed and animal skins of the Greek discipline.

The first 225 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All 12 books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

[Start at Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-1/)

1. [Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-1/) What I Learned, and From Whom
2. [Book II](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-2/)
3. [Book III](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-3/)
4. [Book IV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-4/)
5. [Book V](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-5/)
6. [Book VI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-6/)
7. [Book VII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-7/)
8. [Book VIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-8/)
9. [Book IX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-9/)
10. [Book X](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-10/)
11. [Book XI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-11/)
12. [Book XII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/meditations/book-12/)

## What this edition decided.

The review of November 2026 set these rules for the whole work and applied them. The authority is the Greek. Long and Casaubon are witnesses to it, not sources of text.

- Long's apparatus stays out. Nothing from his square brackets, footnotes, conjectures or ellipses is printed unless the Greek has it. The review found two places where a footnote of Long's had been printed as Marcus's own words: a line of Homer in Book X and Cicero's Latin in Book VII. Both are gone.
- The inner *daimon* is "the divinity within you" every time, so a reader can see it is one thing. Only in VII.17, where the sentence turns on the Greek word, is the word itself named.
- A generic person is "a man" and "he", with "people" for the plural, as the Greek has it. Book VIII had drifted to "a person" and "they" and was brought back.
- Where Marcus quotes the same verse twice, the English is the same twice.
- Where a sentence depends on a Greek pun that English cannot carry, the Greek word is named once inside the sentence. Where English can carry the play, it stays English.
- Quoted speech takes double quotation marks. Quoted verse runs on as prose, because this is a prose edition.

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 3 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. These are all of them, with 1 correction from the review added. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν

The title

**Older:** "Meditations", the traditional title

**Lectio:** Kept as "Meditations", read as "To Himself"

Marcus gave the work no title. "Meditations" is a later editor's label. The Greek means "to himself". The edition keeps the familiar name and treats the text as what it is, a private notebook.

### δαίμων (*daimon*)

Books II, III, V and elsewhere

**Older:** "the daemon" (Long)

**Lectio:** the divinity within you

"Daemon" sends a modern reader toward "demon". For the Stoics it is the share of divine reason each person carries, and Marcus treats it as a god. One phrase throughout lets the reader follow it, and the phrase keeps the word divine.

### τὸ ἡγεμονικόν (*to hegemonikon*)

Throughout

**Older:** "the ruling faculty" (Long)

**Lectio:** the ruling faculty

This is the Stoic name for the part of the self that reasons and commands. Here the edition agrees with Long and keeps his term as the standing one, varying it only where the sentence needs it. The editor has still to decide whether an agreement belongs in a list of divergences.

### τῇ παλλακῇ τοῦ πάππου

Book I, section 17

**Older:** "my grandfather's concubine" (Long)

**Lectio:** my grandfather's mistress

The first draft had "my father's mistress". The Greek says grandfather, and so does Long. It is one of the errors of meaning the review caught, and an example of why every section is read against its sources.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. Three other editions of Meditations are in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **George Long, 1862.** The classic Victorian standard: clear, dignified, widely read.
- **Méric Casaubon, 1634.** The first English Meditations: ornate, archaic, devotional.
- **The original Greek.** The original Koine Greek: Marcus's private notebook (Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν).

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Iliad

Homer

- 800–701 BCE
- Western tradition
- Epic poem
- Lectio Edition 2026

Homer's poem of a few weeks in the tenth year of the war at Troy. It is about what a man does with anger, with grief, and with the certainty that he will die. The Greeks sang it for centuries before anyone wrote it down.

## Homer is fast. The old English versions are slow.

The two public-domain Iliads most people find are Pope's couplets of 1715 and Butler's prose of 1898. Pope is a great English poem and not much like Homer. Butler is plain, but he gives the gods their Roman names and writes "car" for chariot.

A reader who starts either one tends to stop in Book II. The story is not the obstacle. The English is.

The Lectio Edition is a prose Iliad in current English, all twenty-four books. It keeps the repeated epithets, because the repetition is how the poem is built. It restores the Greek names. Pope and Butler stay in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · The Quarrel**

> Rage — sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles, son of Peleus, the ruinous rage that brought the Greeks endless suffering and hurled down to the house of the dead the strong souls of many heroes, leaving their bodies as carrion for the dogs and all the birds — and the will of Zeus was working itself out. Begin where the two first quarreled: Agamemnon, lord of men, and brilliant Achilles.

> Which of the gods set them fighting? Apollo, son of Zeus and Leto. Furious with the king, he sent a foul plague through the camp, and the soldiers were dying — all because Agamemnon had dishonored Chryses, his priest.

> Chryses had come to the fast Greek ships to free his daughter, carrying a boundless ransom, holding in his hands, high on a golden staff, the wreaths of Apollo who strikes from afar. He begged the whole army, but most of all the two sons of Atreus, the marshals of the people:

The first 161 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All 24 books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

[Start at Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-1/)

1. [Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-1/) The Quarrel
2. [Book II](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-2/) The Dream and the Ships
3. [Book III](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-3/) The Duel for Helen
4. [Book IV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-4/) The Broken Truce
5. [Book V](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-5/) The Day of Diomedes
6. [Book VI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-6/) Hector and Andromache
7. [Book VII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-7/) The Duel of Hector and Ajax
8. [Book VIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-8/) The Tide of Battle Turns
9. [Book IX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-9/) The Embassy to Achilles
10. [Book X](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-10/) The Night Raid
11. [Book XI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-11/) The Day of Agamemnon
12. [Book XII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-12/) The Storming of the Wall
13. [Book XIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-13/) Poseidon at the Ships
14. [Book XIV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-14/) The Deception of Zeus
15. [Book XV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-15/) The Battle at the Ships
16. [Book XVI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-16/) The Death of Patroclus
17. [Book XVII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-17/) The Fight over Patroclus
18. [Book XVIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-18/) The Shield of Achilles
19. [Book XIX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-19/) The Rage Laid Down
20. [Book XX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-20/) The Gods Go to War
21. [Book XXI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-21/) The Battle at the River
22. [Book XXII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-22/) The Death of Hector
23. [Book XXIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-23/) The Funeral Games for Patroclus
24. [Book XXIV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/iliad/book-24/) The Ransom of Hector

## What this edition decided.

These are the rules the review settled for the whole poem.

- The first word, *menis*, is "rage". The hot human anger Achilles later curses, *cholos*, is "anger". The two are kept apart, as Homer keeps them.
- The army is mostly "the Greeks". Homer's three names for it, Achaeans, Argives and Danaans, mean the same coalition and were chosen to fit the meter.
- Gods and heroes have their Greek names: Zeus, Hera, Athena, Odysseus.
- Fixed epithets are kept each time they recur: swift-footed Achilles, Hector breaker of horses.
- A patronymic that names a remote ancestor is given as descent. Achilles is "grandson of Aeacus", not his son.
- No Biblical or Christian idiom in a pagan poem, and no modern slang. The draft had "the spirit may be willing", "a time to mourn" and "blowhard". All were replaced with what the Greek says.
- "Car" became "chariot" in 53 places, and leftover archaisms such as "chine" and "a whit" were replaced.

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 73 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 7. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### μῆνις (*menis*)

Book I, line 1

**Older:** "wrath" (Pope), "anger" (Butler)

**Lectio:** rage

The poem's first word. Homer uses it almost only for the anger of gods. "Rage" is the current word nearest to its size.

### Ἀχαιοί, Ἀργεῖοι, Δαναοί

Throughout

**Older:** Achaeans, Argives, Danaans

**Lectio:** the Greeks

Three names for one army. Keeping all three puzzles a new reader and tells him nothing. The introduction records the variety.

### οἵη περ φύλλων γενεή

Book VI, lines 146 to 149

**Older:** "Like leaves on trees the race of man is found" (Pope)

**Lectio:** The generations of men are like the leaves of the trees.

The most quoted lines in the book. Butler has the forest bud with "fresh vines", which is a slip. The Greek is leaves falling and the same tree leafing again.

### οὐ ληϊστή, οὐδ' ἑλετή

Book IX, lines 408 to 409

**Older:** "it can neither be bought nor harried back again" (Butler)

**Lectio:** a man's life cannot be raided back

Achilles uses of his life the same words he has just used of cattle and tripods. Everything Agamemnon offers can be replaced. A life cannot. The edition keeps the raiding words.

### χόλος (*cholos*)

Book XVIII, lines 107 to 110

**Older:** "anger" or "wrath" (Butler, Pope)

**Lectio:** "anger", never "rage"

When Achilles curses the passion that rose in him against Agamemnon, Homer does not use the word of line one. The edition reserves "rage" for *menis* so the reader can feel the difference.

### ἀλλὰ φίλος, θάνε καὶ σύ

Book XXI, line 106

**Older:** "Therefore, my friend, you too shall die" (Butler)

**Lectio:** So die, friend

Achilles calls the boy he is about to kill *philos*, one of his own. He is not being kind. He is counting Lycaon among the doomed, himself included. The address is kept bare.

### Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο

Book XXIV, line 804

**Older:** "And peaceful slept the mighty Hector's shade" (Pope, who rewrites the ending)

**Lectio:** Such was the funeral of Hector, breaker of horses.

The poem ends on Hector, on a burial, and on an epithet. The edition ends where Homer ends.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. Two other editions of The Iliad are in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **Alexander Pope, 1715.** Stately heroic couplets: 18th-century grandeur.
- **Samuel Butler, 1898.** Plain, clear Victorian prose.

The original Greek is not in the bundle yet. Bundling the original for every work is part of the plan, so that review can check against it directly.

## The record for this edition.

Every Lectio edition says how it was made. This one is a beta. It was drafted by an AI model, read against its sources by a second AI reader, and corrected. [The method is described here.](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mission/)

**Status:** [Beta. Open for review.](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#scholars) The first review, by machine readers, is done and its fixes are applied. The readers' review and the editor's own full read have not happened yet. Both come before the release stamp, and only a release is printed.

**Drafted:** June 15, 2026, by Claude Opus 4.8 (`claude-opus-4-8`), an AI model. 24 books, about 148,400 words.

**Revised:** November 17, 2026

- Samuel Butler, prose (1898, public domain)
- Lang, Leaf & Myers, prose (1882, public domain)

- the Greek (Homeric text)

**First review:** November 2026. 24 books read against Butler (1898) and Pope (1715). The Greek is not in the bundle, so the Greek readings came from the reviewing model's own knowledge of the text. 4 graded A, 20 graded B, none graded C.

**Fixes applied:** 163: 5 high (meaning), 44 medium (a reader would stumble), 114 low (polish). Each was re-checked by a further pass before it was applied.

### Still open

What the first review left for the editor to decide or restore.

- The editor's own read of all twenty-four books.
- Book I: Achilles' retelling of the quarrel to Thetis is 28 lines of speech in Homer. The edition still gives it as a short narrated list. It has to be restored as speech, and that is new writing the editor should read.
- Three segments are set aside, in Books V, X and XXIII. The editor has to decide whether to retire them for good or replace them with Homer's own closing lines.
- The note that stood at the end of Book XXIII should move to the margin notes.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Odyssey

Homer

- 800–701 BCE
- Western tradition
- Epic poem
- Lectio Edition 2026

Homer's poem of the long way home. Odysseus spends ten years getting back from Troy to his wife, his son and his island. Under the monsters and the gods it is about cunning, endurance and the pull of home.

## The story is easy. The 1900 file is not.

The free Odyssey is Samuel Butler's prose of 1900. Butler is readable, but he calls the hero Ulysses and the goddess Minerva, and he flattens the repeated lines that give the poem its sound.

The Lectio Edition tells all twenty-four books in current English. It keeps the Greek names and the fixed epithets, and where Homer repeats a line word for word, so does the English. Butler stays in the app beside it.

It was made to be read alongside the Lectio Iliad. The two share their names, their epithets and their spelling.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · Athena Visits Ithaca**

> Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns — the one who wandered far and long after he sacked the holy city of Troy. He saw the cities of many peoples and learned how they thought; he suffered deep grief on the open sea, fighting for his own life and for the safe homecoming of his men. But he could not save them, hard as he tried — they died by their own reckless folly, those fools, when they devoured the cattle of Hyperion the Sun, who took from them the day of their return. Of these things, goddess, daughter of Zeus, begin where you will, and tell us too.

> By now everyone who had escaped a violent death — in the war or on the sea — was home. Only Odysseus was still kept from his wife and his own country, held back by the nymph Calypso, a queen among goddesses, who wanted him for a husband and kept him deep inside her hollow cave. And when at last, as the years rolled on, the time came that the gods had spun for him to return to Ithaca, his trials were still not over, not even among his own people. The gods pitied him now — all of them but Poseidon, who stayed furious with godlike Odysseus and would not let him reach his homeland.

The first 227 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All 24 books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

24. [Book XXIV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/odyssey/book-24/) Peace in Ithaca

## What this edition decided.

The review swept all twenty-four books for each of these and corrected every departure it found.

- Gods and heroes keep their Greek names, in the familiar Latinized spelling: Odysseus, Athena, Telemachus, Eurycleia. The draft had mixed spellings such as Antinoos and Antinous. One form now holds.
- The army is "the Greeks", as in the Iliad.
- Fixed epithets have one form each: "winged words", "gray-eyed Athena", "Zeus who gathers the clouds", "earth-shaker".
- Lines Homer repeats word for word are rendered word for word. Penelope's shroud speech is the same in Books II, XIX and XXIV.
- Homeric idioms are kept where English can carry them and translated where it cannot.
- Modern idioms with the wrong sense came out: "make your play", "good luck to you", "last supper". So did leftover archaisms such as "trumpery" and "steading".

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 72 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 5, with 1 correction from the review added. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### πολύτροπος (*polytropos*)

Book I, line 1

**Older:** "that ingenious hero" (Butler)

**Lectio:** the man of many turns

The word means both much-traveled and quick to turn in thought. Older versions pick one sense. The phrase holds both.

### πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς

Throughout

**Older:** "the much-enduring noble Odysseus"

**Lectio:** long-suffering Odysseus

His standing epithet. Endurance is what defines him, and the reader should hear it each time Homer says it.

### Οὖτις (*Outis*)

Book IX, lines 366 to 414

**Older:** "Noman" (Butler, Pope)

**Lectio:** Nobody

Odysseus names himself Nobody, so that when the Cyclops shouts that Nobody is killing him, his neighbors go home. The name has to be the same word in the cave and in the cry, and it has to be ordinary English.

### ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ

Book XI, lines 489 to 491

**Older:** "a paid servant in a poor man's house" (Butler)

**Lectio:** I would rather be a hired hand, working another man's land

Achilles among the dead takes back the creed of the Iliad. The Greek is exact: a hired field hand serving a man who has no land of his own. He is free, and he is at the bottom. "Servant" is too vague.

### τέτλαθι δή, κραδίη

Book XX, line 18

**Older:** "Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear" (Butler)

**Lectio:** Endure, my heart. You have borne worse than this.

The verb is from the same root as his epithet. He is ordering himself to be what his name says he is.

### ἔπεα πτερόεντα

Throughout

**Older:** varied

**Lectio:** winged words

The draft gave this formula several ways. Homer gives it one way. Eleven places were corrected.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. One other edition of The Odyssey is in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **Samuel Butler, 1900.** Plain, clear Victorian prose.

The original Greek is not in the bundle yet. Bundling the original for every work is part of the plan, so that review can check against it directly.

## The record for this edition.

Every Lectio edition says how it was made. This one is a beta. It was drafted by an AI model, read against its sources by a second AI reader, and corrected. [The method is described here.](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/mission/)

**Status:** [Beta. Open for review.](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/#scholars) The first review, by machine readers, is done and its fixes are applied. The readers' review and the editor's own full read have not happened yet. Both come before the release stamp, and only a release is printed.

**Drafted:** June 16, 2026, by Claude Opus 4.8 (`claude-opus-4-8`), an AI model. 24 books, about 118,400 words.

**Vintage:** 2026

**Revised:** November 17, 2026

**Sources:**

- Samuel Butler, prose (1900, public domain)
- Butcher & Lang, prose (1879, public domain)
- Robert Fitzgerald (1961, consulted)
- Robert Fagles (1996, consulted)
- Emily Wilson (2017, consulted)
- the Greek (Homeric text)

**First review:** November 2026. 24 books read against Butler (1900). The Greek is not in the bundle, so the Greek readings came from the reviewing model's own knowledge of the text. 5 graded A, 19 graded B, none graded C.

**Fixes applied:** 283: 2 high (meaning), 31 medium (a reader would stumble), 250 low (polish). Each was re-checked by a further pass before it was applied.

**Set aside:** 2 segments that held an editor's note or an invented sentence, not the author's text, are marked to be skipped by the app, print and audio.

### Still open

What the first review left for the editor to decide or restore.

- The editor's own read of all twenty-four books.
- Seven lines about Helen in Penelope's speech (Book XXIII) were missing and have been restored. Ancient critics doubted these lines. The edition has no note saying so yet.
- Two translator's notes that had been printed as Homer's text, in Books V and XIV, are set aside. The first belongs in the margin notes. The second made a false claim and must be reworded before it goes anywhere.
- A passage in Book XVII repeats one in Book IV and is still worded differently. Matching them is optional.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Republic

Plato

- 375 BCE
- Western tradition
- Philosophy
- Lectio Edition 2026

Plato's dialogue on justice. Socrates asks what justice is and whether it is worth having, and to answer he builds a city in words. The Cave, the divided line and the philosopher-king all come from this book.

## It is a conversation, and it should read like one.

Benjamin Jowett's translation of 1871 is lucid and long-lived. It is also Victorian. His speakers swear "By heaven", his Cave is a "den", and his key words have moved since he chose them. "Temperance" now means not drinking. "Idea" now means a thought in someone's head.

The Lectio Edition renders all ten books as talk between people, in current English, and fixes one English word for each term the argument turns on. Jowett stays in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · What Is Justice?**

> I went down to the Piraeus yesterday with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, to offer my prayers to the goddess, and to see how they would put on the festival, this being the first time it was held. I thought the procession our own people made was beautiful, though the one the Thracians marched in looked every bit as good. We said our prayers, watched the spectacle, and set off back toward the city. And just then Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, caught sight of us from a distance, starting on the road home, and sent his slave running ahead to tell us to wait for him. The boy caught my cloak from behind and said: Polemarchus asks you to wait.

> I turned around and asked where his master was.

> There he is, said the boy — coming up behind you. Just wait.

> Of course we'll wait, said Glaucon; and in a few minutes Polemarchus came up, with Adeimantus, Glaucon's brother, Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others, all on their way from the procession.

The first 176 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All ten books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

[Start at Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-1/)

2. [Book II](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-2/) The Ring of Gyges
3. [Book III](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-3/) The Noble Lie
4. [Book IV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-4/) Justice Found
5. [Book V](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-5/) The Three Waves
6. [Book VI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-6/) The Sun and the Divided Line
7. [Book VII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-7/) The Cave
8. [Book VIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-8/) The Decay of Regimes
9. [Book IX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-9/) The Tyrant's Soul
10. [Book X](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/republic/book-10/) Poetry and the Myth of Er

## What this edition decided.

The review found that this edition's terms drifted from book to book. These are the rules that now hold.

- Explanations are never printed as Plato's text. A gloss on a name, a pun or an allusion comes out of the sentence and goes to the margin notes. The review found a translator's note inside the Muses' speech in Book VIII.
- The four virtues are wisdom, courage, self-command and justice. *Sophrosyne* had been "self-discipline", "self-restraint" and "temperance" in different books.
- *Gymnastike* is "physical training". "Gymnastics" now means a sport.
- When the Greek swears by Zeus, the English says "by Zeus". "God" and "Good lord" are not used as exclamations.
- A line of Homer quoted twice has one wording.
- Words that date the text came out: "girlfriend", "the haves", "consumer", "payroll", "the gym".

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 30 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 7. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον

Book I, 338c

**Older:** "justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger

"Interest" has drifted toward finance and polite concern. "Advantage" keeps Thrasymachus as blunt as Plato makes him.

### γενναῖόν τι ἓν ψευδομένους

Book III, 414b

**Older:** "just one royal lie" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** One noble lie

*Gennaios* means well-born. Plato's phrase is a contradiction on purpose, a lie of good family. "Royal" names who hears the lie. "Noble" keeps the discomfort.

### σωφροσύνη (*sophrosyne*)

Book IV and throughout

**Older:** "temperance" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** self-command

Plato explains the word by the phrase "stronger than himself": the better part of a man holding the worse. "Self-command" keeps that in view each time.

### ἐὰν μὴ οἱ φιλόσοφοι βασιλεύσωσιν

Book V, 473c

**Older:** "Until philosophers are kings" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** Unless philosophers become kings in our cities

The Greek is a hard condition and promises nothing. "Until" tells the reader the day is coming. Plato does not say so.

### καταγείῳ οἰκήσει σπηλαιώδει

Book VII, 514a

**Older:** "an underground den" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** a kind of cave

A den is where an animal lives. The image depends on its being a place where people live and which they take for the world.

### ἡ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἰδέα

Book VII

**Older:** "the idea of good" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** the form of the good

To a modern ear an idea is a thought. Plato means the opposite: the thing most real, seen last and with effort.

### δαίμων (*daimon*)

Book X, 617e

**Older:** "genius" (Jowett)

**Lectio:** guardian spirit

"Genius" now means talent. The *daimon* is the spirit that goes with a life. In the myth of Er the soul chooses its own, which is why the blame is the chooser's.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. One other edition of The Republic is in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **Benjamin Jowett, 1871.** The classic Victorian Republic: Jowett's lucid, hugely influential standard.

The original Greek is not in the bundle yet. Bundling the original for every work is part of the plan, so that review can check against it directly.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Aeneid

Virgil

- 29–19 BCE
- Western tradition
- Epic poem
- Lectio Edition 2026

Virgil's epic of Rome. Aeneas carries his father and his household gods out of burning Troy and goes to found the people who will become Rome. It is a poem about duty and about what duty costs.

## Dryden is a monument. He is not an on-ramp.

The public-domain Aeneid is John Dryden's verse of 1697. It is one of the great English translations, and it is in couplets more than three centuries old. Dryden also paraphrases freely. "I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts" becomes "Trust not their presents, nor admit the horse".

The Lectio Edition gives the twelve books as prose in current English. It keeps Virgil's names and keeps each famous line at its own length and shape. Dryden stays in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · The Storm, and Carthage**

> Arms, and the man, I sing — the man who, driven by fate, was first to flee the shores of Troy and come to Italy and its Lavinian coast. He was battered hard over sea and land by the power of the gods, for cruel Juno's unforgetting rage hounded him at every turn; and bitter were the wars he fought before he could found his city and carry his gods into Latium. From him came the Latin people, the Alban fathers, and the high walls of Rome.

> Muse, tell me the causes. What wound to her divinity, what burning grievance, drove the queen of heaven to force a man so faithful, so devoted, through such a gauntlet of disaster — to hurl one trouble after another in his path? Can there really be such anger in the hearts of gods?

> There was an ancient city, Carthage, a colony out of Tyre, facing Italy far across the water, opposite the mouth of the Tiber — a city rich in resources and fierce in the arts of war. They say Juno loved it above all places on earth, more even than Samos. Here she kept her armor; here she kept her chariot. And it was her fixed ambition, if fate would only allow it, that this city should one day rule the world.

The first 221 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All 12 books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

[Start at Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-1/)

1. [Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-1/) The Storm, and Carthage
2. [Book II](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-2/) The Fall of Troy
3. [Book III](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-3/) The Wanderings, and the Death of Anchises
4. [Book IV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-4/) The Tragedy of Dido
5. [Book V](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-5/) The Games for Anchises, and the Loss of Palinurus
6. [Book VI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-6/) The Descent to the Underworld
7. [Book VII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-7/) Latium, and the Opening of the War

10. [Book X](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-10/) The Council of the Gods, the Death of Pallas, and the End of Mezentius
11. [Book XI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/aeneid/book-11/) The Death of Pallas, the Council, and Camilla

## What this edition decided.

The review set these rules and applied them across the twelve books.

- Names are the ones Virgil gives, in his Latin forms: Minerva, never Athena. Tartarus, Erebus and Dis, where the draft had put "hell". No name is added that Virgil leaves out, and none is dropped.
- No oaths to one God in a poem with many gods. A character swears by Jupiter or simply cries out.
- No modern idiom that calls up something outside the poem. The draft had "gone with the wind" and "for free".
- The poet's narration does not use contractions. Direct speech may, when the speaker is talking in the moment. Prayers, oaths and prophecy do not.
- Famous lines keep their own length and shape.
- The last line of Book XI and the last line of the poem are the same line in Latin, and are now the same in English.

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 36 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 7. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### *pietas*

Throughout

**Older:** "piety", "pious Aeneas"

**Lectio:** "duty", "dutiful Aeneas"

*Pietas* is what a man owes to gods, country and family. "Piety" now means religious feeling. "Duty" is what drives Aeneas, and what the poem counts the cost of.

### *timeo Danaos et dona ferentis*

Book II, line 49

**Older:** "Trust not their presents, nor admit the horse" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** I fear the Greeks even when they come bearing gifts

The line is a proverb in English already. The edition keeps it close to the shape people know.

### *agnosco veteris vestigia flammae*

Book IV, line 23

**Older:** "Too like the sparkles of my former flame" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** I recognize the marks of the old flame

Dido admits she loves again. *Vestigia* are traces, footprints, a scar. Dryden's "sparkles" is prettier than the Latin.

### *hoc opus, hic labor est*

Book VI, lines 126 to 129

**Older:** "In this the task and mighty labour lies" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** that is the labor, that is the task

Anyone can go down. Coming back is the hard part. The descent to the underworld is built on that contrast, and the doubled close is kept.

### *parcere subiectis et debellare superbos*

Book VI, lines 851 to 853

**Older:** "To tame the proud, the fetter'd slave to free" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** to spare the conquered, and to crush the proud

Virgil's statement of what Rome is for. Dryden softens the second half. The edition leaves the cost where Virgil put it.

### *flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo*

Book VII, line 312

**Older:** "Hell shall the pow'r of Heav'n and Jove supply" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** If I cannot bend the gods above, I will stir up Hell

Juno's vow in two plain halves. Note that this line still says "Hell", against the edition's own rule on names. It is on the editor's list below.

### *vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras*

Book XII, line 952

**Older:** "And the disdainful soul came rushing through the wound" (Dryden)

**Lectio:** and life fled with a groan, resentful, down to the shades

The last line. The poem ends on the kill, with no funeral and no peace. The same line closes Camilla's death in Book XI and is rendered the same way there.

- **John Dryden, 1697.** Stately heroic couplets: the great English Virgil.

- Three of the edition's notes quote wording the text no longer has, including the notes on the first line and on *sunt lacrimae rerum*. They need rewriting.
- Prayers and speeches of state in Books IX to XII have not been checked one by one for contractions.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Prince

Niccolò Machiavelli

- 1513
- Western tradition
- Politics
- Lectio Edition 2026

A short handbook on power, written in 1513 by a Florentine diplomat who had lost his post. Machiavelli sets aside how rulers ought to behave and describes what they must do to keep a state.

## One word carries the book, and the old translation hides it.

The standard free translation is W. K. Marriott's of 1908. It is clear and faithful. But Machiavelli runs his whole argument on one word, *virtù*, and Marriott turns it into a different English word almost every time: ability, valour, energy, talent.

A reader of Marriott cannot see that the book is one argument about one quality set against fortune. A reader of the Italian cannot miss it.

The Lectio Edition renders the twenty-six chapters in current English and leaves *virtù* in Italian wherever Machiavelli uses it in this sense. Marriott stays in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Chapter I · The Kinds of Principalities**

> All states, all dominions that have held and hold power over men, have been and are either republics or principalities.

> Principalities are either hereditary, where one bloodline has ruled for a long time, or they are new.

> The new ones are either new outright, as Milan was to Francesco Sforza, or they are like limbs grafted onto the hereditary state of the prince who acquires them, as the kingdom of Naples is to the King of Spain.

> Dominions acquired this way are accustomed either to living under a prince or to being free; and they are acquired either with the arms of others or with one's own, either by fortune or by virtù.

> **Chapter II · Hereditary Principalities**

> I will leave republics aside, since I have discussed them at length elsewhere. I will turn only to principalities, taking up the threads laid out above, and ask how these principalities can be governed and kept.

> I say at once that hereditary states, accustomed to the bloodline of their prince, are far less difficult to hold than new ones. It is enough not to break the customs of one's ancestors, and to play for time when events turn; then a prince of ordinary industry will always keep his state, unless some extraordinary and overwhelming force strips him of it — and even stripped of it, he wins it back the moment the usurper stumbles.

The first 227 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

22. [Chapter XXII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/chapter-22/) A Prince's Ministers
23. [Chapter XXIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/chapter-23/) Avoiding Flatterers
24. [Chapter XXIV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/chapter-24/) Why Italy's Princes Lost Their States
25. [Chapter XXV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/chapter-25/) Fortune, and How to Resist Her
26. [Chapter XXVI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/the-prince/chapter-26/) Exhortation to Free Italy

## What this edition decided.

The review graded twenty of twenty-six chapters as needing no change. The rules it set are few.

- *Virtù* stays untranslated from Chapter I to Chapter XXVI. It means skill, force and nerve together, with no moral content. No single English word holds it, and five different English words hide that it is one idea. The draft had kept it in some chapters and translated it in others.
- The adjective *virtuoso* is "able". The ordinary moral plural, virtues set against vices, stays English.
- *Spegnere*, to put out a flame, is "snuff out" each time Machiavelli uses it of a family or a republic.
- No explanation is written into Machiavelli's sentence. The draft defined *virtù* inside Chapter I and glossed the Parlement of Paris inside Chapter XIX. Both glosses were removed.
- Roman Gaul is Gaul, not France. Names carry their accents: Forlì, Vailà.

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 62 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 7. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### *o per fortuna o per virtù*

Chapter I

**Older:** "or else by fortune or by ability" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** either by fortune or by virtù

The first appearance of the pair the whole book is built on. The Italian word is kept here and at every later use.

### *o vezzeggiare o spegnere*

Chapter III

**Older:** "either to be well treated or crushed" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** men should be either treated well or snuffed out

The verb is the one for putting out a flame. Keeping the image, and keeping it the same each time, lets the reader hear the maxim return.

### *Non si può ancora chiamare virtù*

Chapter VIII

**Older:** "Yet it cannot be called talent to slay fellow-citizens" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** it cannot be called virtù to kill your fellow citizens

The one sentence where Machiavelli refuses his own word to a man who seems to have earned it. "Talent" loses the refusal.

### *la verità effettuale della cosa*

Chapter XV

**Older:** "the real truth of the matter" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** the effectual truth of the thing

Machiavelli coined the phrase: truth measured by what works. "Real truth" makes it ordinary emphasis. The edition keeps it strange.

### *imparare a potere essere non buono*

Chapter XV

**Older:** "to know how to do wrong" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** to learn how not to be good

Marriott moralizes. Machiavelli says the prince must be able to be not good, and use that or not as need requires.

### *la fortuna è donna*

Chapter XXV

**Older:** "it is necessary to beat and ill-use her" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her down you must beat her and shove her

The most notorious sentence in the book, at full force. Softening it would misreport the writer. The reader should meet it as written and judge him.

### *il parlamento e la sua autorità*

Chapter XIX

**Older:** "the parliament and its authority" (Marriott)

**Lectio:** the Parlement and its authority

He means the Parlement of Paris, a court of law. "Parliament" suggests a legislature, which it was not. The French name marks the difference.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. One other edition of The Prince is in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **W. K. Marriott, 1908.** The standard public-domain Prince: Marriott's clear, faithful Edwardian English.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Analects

Confucius

- 479–221 BCE
- Eastern tradition
- Philosophy
- Lectio Edition 2026

The sayings and conversations of Confucius, written down by his students after his death. Twenty short books on learning, ritual, family, government, and what it takes to become fully human.

## The sayings are short. The Victorian English is not.

James Legge's translation of 1893 is the scholar's standard and it is careful. It is also wordy where the Chinese is brief. Two plain words in the original become "to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others".

Legge also renders the book's central word, *ren*, as a general "virtue", so a reader cannot follow it. And his "superior man" sounds like rank, which is the opposite of what Confucius meant.

The Lectio Edition keeps each saying about the size the Chinese keeps it, and gives each key term one English word. Legge stays in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Book I · Learning**

> The Master said, "To learn, and in good time to practice what you have learned — is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from far away — is that not a joy? To go unrecognized and feel no bitterness — is that not a gentleman?"

> Master Yu said, "Men who honor their parents and respect their elder brothers rarely have a taste for defying their superiors, and no man without that taste has ever been fond of stirring up revolt. The gentleman tends to the root; when the root is set, the Way grows from it. Devotion to parents and respect for elders — surely these are the root of human-heartedness."

> The Master said, "Clever words and a winning face rarely keep company with human-heartedness."

> Master Tsang said, "Each day I examine myself on three points. Working for others, was I faithless? With my friends, did I fail to keep my word? What was handed on to me, did I leave unpracticed?"

The first 164 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.

## The whole edition is here to read.

All 20 books, free, one page each. It is the same text the app reads, and it is a beta, so it will be corrected as the review goes on.

[Start at Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-1/)

1. [Book I](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-1/) Learning
2. [Book II](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-2/) Governing
3. [Book III](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-3/) Eight Rows of Dancers
4. [Book IV](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-4/) Human-Heartedness
5. [Book V](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-5/) Weighing Men
6. [Book VI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-6/) Knowing, Loving, Delighting
7. [Book VII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-7/) The Transmitter
8. [Book VIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-8/) A Heavy Load, a Long Road
9. [Book IX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-9/) The Passing Stream
10. [Book X](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-10/) At Home and at Court
11. [Book XI](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-11/) Men of Former Times

18. [Book XVIII](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-18/) The Viscount of Wei
19. [Book XIX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-19/) Tsze-chang
20. [Book XX](https://sandiegotech.org/lectio/analects/book-20/) Yao Said

## What this edition decided.

The review graded fourteen of twenty books as needing no change. Most of its fixes were to punctuation. The edition's main choices are in its terms.

- *Ren* is "human-heartedness" everywhere. "Virtue" is kept for *de*, moral force, so the reader can watch the two ideas separately.
- *Junzi* is "the gentleman": a man defined by conduct, not birth.
- *Li* is "ritual", one word throughout.
- Explanations are not written into the Master's sentences. Glosses the draft had added in Books V, XI and XIV were removed.
- Proper names follow Legge's romanization, so the edition and the 1893 text can be read side by side.
- One style of quotation mark across all twenty books. Books VI to X had used a different one.

### Where it differs from the older translations

The edition records 48 divergences: places where it departs from the older English, each with its reason. Here are 8. The full record is in the app, one tap from the text.

### 仁 (*ren*)

Book I and throughout

**Older:** "true virtue", "perfect virtue", "benevolent actions" (Legge)

**Lectio:** human-heartedness

*Ren* is the particular excellence of being fully human toward other people, and it is the book's central word. Legge folds it into "virtue" and it disappears.

### 君子 (*junzi*)

Book I and throughout

**Older:** "the superior man" (Legge)

**Lectio:** the gentleman

The word once meant a lord's son. Confucius remade it to mean a formed character, open to anyone who does the work. "Gentleman" has made the same journey in English.

### 禮 (*li*)

Book III and throughout

**Older:** "the rules of propriety" (Legge)

**Lectio:** ritual

Legge makes it sound like a code of etiquette. *Li* is rite, ceremony and the learned forms respect takes, all as one thing.

### 忠恕 (*zhong shu*)

Book IV

**Older:** "to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others" (Legge)

**Lectio:** loyalty, and putting yourself in the other man's place

The one thread through the Master's Way is two plain words. The edition keeps it that size.

### 子不語怪，力，亂，神

Book VII, 20

**Older:** "extraordinary things, feats of strength, disorder, and spiritual beings" (Legge)

**Lectio:** The Master did not speak of marvels, feats of strength, rebellion, or the spirits.

Four bare words in the Chinese. *Luan* in this company is political violence, not untidiness.

### 過猶不及

Book XI

**Older:** "To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short" (Legge)

**Lectio:** Too far is no better than not far enough.

The proverb weighs the same on both sides and uses no moral word. Legge's "wrong" adds a judgment the Chinese leaves out.

### 己所不欲，勿施於人

Book XII

**Older:** "not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself" (Legge)

**Lectio:** What you do not want done to you, do not do to others.

The golden rule in its negative form, five centuries before the positive one. In the Chinese it is a free-standing command of eight characters, and it returns in Book XV.

### 君子和而不同

Book XIII

**Older:** "The superior man is affable, but not adulatory" (Legge)

**Lectio:** The gentleman is in harmony without being in unison.

These are music words. Harmony is different notes agreeing. Unison is one note doubled. Legge moves the saying into drawing-room manners.

## The other editions on hand.

The Lectio Edition is what opens by default. One other edition of The Analects is in the bundle, and switching keeps your place.

- **James Legge, 1893.** The scholar's Analects: Legge's careful, literal Victorian standard.

The original Classical Chinese is not in the bundle yet. Bundling the original for every work is part of the plan, so that review can check against it directly.

Lectio Edition · 2026

# The Tao Te Ching

Laozi

- 400–301 BCE
- Eastern tradition
- Philosophy
- Lectio Edition 2026

Eighty-one short chapters, part poem and part proverb, ascribed to Laozi. They teach the Way that cannot be named and the power that works by yielding. It is the founding text of Taoism.

## A book this short should not need brackets.

James Legge's translation of 1891 is exact and hard to read. He explains inside the line, in brackets: "The highest excellence is like (that of) water." He reads the famous first line as a path one can walk, which loses its argument about speech and names.

The Chinese is spare, and it hedges where it is unsure. A translation that explains and decides for it is a different book.

The Lectio Edition gives each chapter in a few plain sentences, with no gloss inside the line, and keeps the hedges where the Chinese has them. Legge stays in the app beside it.

## How it begins.

> **Chapter 1 · The Way and the Name**

> The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.

> Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.

> So if you are always without desire, you see its hidden depths; but if desire is always in you, you see only its outer edges.

> These two spring from the same source, though we call them by different names. Together they are the Mystery — mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

> **Chapter 2 · The Mutual Arising of Opposites**

> When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared. When everyone recognizes good as good, what is not good has already appeared.

> So it is that being and non-being give rise to each other; the difficult and the easy complete each other; the long and the short measure each other; the high and the low lean on each other; note and voice harmonize with each other; before and after follow each other.

The first 172 words of the Lectio Edition, as they stand in the bundle the app reads.
